svg.title: Inside 3D NAND: a vertical string, one charge-trap cell, and why more bits per cell shrink the margins
svg.desc: Left: a vertical cross-section of one 3D NAND string. A bit line sits on top, then a drain select gate, a tall stack of word-line plates separated by oxide, a source select gate and the source line, with CMOS logic under or bonded to the array. A vertical channel hole runs through all the word lines. During a read, the selected word line gets a reference voltage while every other word line gets a pass voltage, which slowly disturbs them. Middle: a top-down slice of one charge-trap cell, showing concentric rings: tungsten word line, blocking oxide, silicon-nitride charge-trap layer, tunnel oxide, polysilicon channel and oxide core. Programming pulls electrons through the tunnel oxide into the trap layer; erasing injects holes from the channel that neutralise the stored charge, for a whole block at once; every cycle damages the tunnel oxide. Right: threshold-voltage distributions for SLC, TLC and QLC in the same voltage window, showing 2, 8 and 16 states with progressively narrower gaps.
svg.text: Inside 3D NAND: string, cell and voltage states
Schematic, not to scale. Original drawing for the Everpure Tech Atlas, Chapter 2.
CMOS periphery under, or bonded to, the array
Cells in a string sit in series. Reading one
cell turns all the others on with a pass
Tunnel oxide: wears with each P/E cycle
Program: word-line pulses push electrons into
the trap layer, raising the threshold voltage.
Erase: a high channel voltage injects holes
that cancel the charge, whole block at once.
Threshold voltage → (fixed window of a few volts)
Each extra bit doubles the states in the
same window, so gaps roughly halve. Cells
stronger ECC, and they tolerate less
